name: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
title: Dialogue Engines and Virtual Docents
answer: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are conversational systems that guide visitors through exhibitions, installations, and online art spaces. They combine natural language processing with character design to answer questions, offer context, and shape a visitor's path. In interactive and experiential art, they often act as performers or hosts, blurring the line between artwork and interface. The field sits within The Art of AI, where the docent is both a tool and a subject of the work.

sections.body: Dialogue engines and virtual docents are conversational systems that guide visitors through exhibitions, installations, and online art spaces. They combine natural language processing with character design to answer questions, offer context, and shape a visitor's path. In interactive and experiential art, they often act as performers or hosts, blurring the line between artwork and interface. The field sits within The Art of AI, where the docent is both a tool and a subject of the work.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a stack of speech recognition, language understanding, dialogue management, and speech synthesis. They may use cloud APIs or local models, and they often rely on audio models for voice input and output. The site tracks 2000 audio models, which reflects the breadth of voice technology available to artists and developers. Hardware ranges from a smartphone to a gallery installation with microphones, speakers, and a screen.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with writing a character, a knowledge base, and a set of conversational goals. Developers then choose a dialogue engine, which might be a large language model with retrieval augmented generation, a rule-based system, or a hybrid. They test the docent with real visitors, refine prompts and fallback responses, and often add a human operator for edge cases. Iteration is constant because dialogue is unpredictable and art spaces are noisy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on voice cloning, training data, and the provenance of generated answers. A virtual docent may speak in a cloned voice, which raises consent and licensing questions, and its knowledge may come from copyrighted texts or living artists. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits across AI, a sign that these issues are far from settled. Artists and institutions also need to consider privacy, bias, and transparency, especially when a docent collects visitor data. Provenance tools and clear disclosure help, but they are not a complete solution.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The next steps include more embodied docents, with gestures, gaze, and movement in physical space. Multimodal models will let a docent see a visitor's expression and respond to it, while memory systems will allow continuity across visits. We can expect tighter integration with augmented and virtual reality, and more artist-led experiments that treat the docent as a character with its own agency. Ethical frameworks and audience expectations will evolve alongside the technology, shaping what a virtual docent is allowed to say and do.
